name: Pilates

lead: Pilates is a low-impact exercise system built around controlled movement, breathing and core engagement. People use it to strengthen the trunk, line the body up better and carry a more upright, toned look.

The chain is a stronger core, better alignment, then an upright, toned appearance. Joseph Pilates developed it in the early twentieth century as Contrology. Network meta-analyses of exercise for chronic low back pain include Pilates among effective types, and reviews cited on Wikipedia describe low-quality evidence that it beats no exercise for low back pain but is no better than other exercise. No study found tests it for posture appearance.

paras: It is done on a mat or on spring-based apparatus such as the Reformer, in classes or private sessions, commonly two or three times a week. Many people pair it with lifting or cardio. Gains in core control and body awareness build over weeks of regular sessions.

It is low-impact and the sources reviewed describe no significant harms. It has not been shown to treat medical conditions. People with existing spine or joint problems may want to let an instructor know.

Pilates: Flexibility yes, weight loss no

angle.text: Pilates builds core control and alignment, which people use to carry a more upright, toned look. It runs from a stronger trunk to better alignment to a tidier posture. Reviews show back-pain benefit similar to other exercise; posture appearance has not been tested directly.

lead: Pilates is a mind-body exercise system named for Joseph Pilates, who developed it in the first half of the twentieth century and called it Contrology. He said the idea arose during his World War I internment on the Isle of Man, and published Your Health (1934) and Return to Life Through Contrology (1945).[1][2] It emphasises core stability, breathing, alignment and flexibility, performed on a mat or on apparatus such as the Reformer and Cadillac.[1][2]

A systematic review noted the difficulty of defining Pilates exercise consistently across studies.[3] Network meta-analyses of exercise for chronic low back pain include Pilates among effective modes, and Wikipedia reports low-quality evidence that it beats no exercise but is no better than other exercise.[1][4][5] No study found tests Pilates for changing posture appearance.
infobox: Mat; Reformer, Cadillac, Wunda Chair, barrels
Low back pain: similar to other exercise

paras: Joseph Pilates, born in 1883 near Dusseldorf, reportedly refined his methods during WWI internment, rigging hospital beds with springs for recovering patients, and emigrated to New York in 1926 where his studio drew dancers.[2] Early students including Romana Kryzanowska and Ron Fletcher spread the method, and modern and classical styles now coexist.[1]

A 2006 randomised controlled trial studied Pilates-based therapeutic exercise in people with nonspecific chronic low back pain and functional disability.[6] A 2020 network meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine of 89 trials examined which exercise modes best treat nonspecific chronic low back pain, and a 2022 network meta-analysis compared Pilates, strength, core-based and mind-body exercise.[4][5] A 2021 network meta-analysis in the Journal of Physiotherapy reported some exercise types are more effective than others for chronic low back pain.[7]

A 2010 randomised study examined Pilates in women with breast cancer, and a 2017 Cochrane overview covered physical activity and exercise for chronic pain generally.[8][9] Wikipedia notes a 2015 Australian review found Pilates evidence uncertain because studies were few and methodologically limited, and that it has not been shown to be an effective treatment for any medical condition.[1] No studies found testing Pilates for visible posture or appearance change.

timeline.event: Joseph Pilates emigrates to New York and opens a studio.[2]
Return to Life Through Contrology published.[1]
